hints: Expand both compound sines and add them so opposite terms cancel.
walkthrough:
Expand $\sin(3x + 2x)$ using the compound angle formula:
$$\sin(3x + 2x) = \sin 3x\cos 2x + \cos 3x\sin 2x$$

Expand $\sin(3x - 2x)$ using the compound angle formula:
$$\sin(3x - 2x) = \sin 3x\cos 2x - \cos 3x\sin 2x$$

Add the two expansions together:
$$\sin(3x + 2x) + \sin(3x - 2x) = 2\sin 3x\cos 2x$$
$$\sin 5x + \sin x = 2\sin 3x\cos 2x$$

Multiply by $\dfrac{1}{2}$ to obtain the required identity:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}(\sin 5x + \sin x) \equiv \sin 3x\cos 2x$$
This completes the proof.

hints: Replace the integrand using the identity from part (a).
Integrate $\frac12(\sin5x+\sin x)$, apply $0$ and $\pi/4$, and use exact cosine values.
walkthrough:
Rewrite the integral using the identity established in part (a):
$$\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \sin 3x\cos 2x\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} (\sin 5x + \sin x)\,\mathrm{d}x$$

Evaluate at the upper limit $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\cos\left(5 \times \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \cos\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{4}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$$
$$\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$$
Upper limit value:
$$-\dfrac{-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}}{5} - \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{10} - \dfrac{5\sqrt{2}}{10} = -\dfrac{4\sqrt{2}}{10} = -\dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{5}$$

Subtract the lower limit value from the upper limit value:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\left[-\dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{5} - \left(-\dfrac{6}{5}\right)\right] = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{6 - 2\sqrt{2}}{5}\right) = \dfrac{3 - \sqrt{2}}{5} = \dfrac{1}{5}(3 - \sqrt{2})$$
This completes the proof.
